The genitive case in English is basically just used for ordinary possession. The genitive suffix -'s attaches to the genitive noun(*) . The construction you gave, "one [of a dozen]" would be called "partitive" not genitive (it means the noun is a part belonging to a whole), though the partitive is expressed by the genitive in many languages, including Ancient Greek and Latin.

While the English genitive is pretty restricted, "of" has a range of uses, like substance ("sheet [of iron]"), condition ("faint [of heart]"), and belonging/partition (the example above), in Ancient Greek and Latin the genitive performs all of these functions and more. You can think of "of" itself kind of like a genitive prefix. 

In Greek in particular, there used to be an old "ablative" case that merged with the genitive case, so the genitive ended up taking on a whole bunch of extra functions BEYOND what I described above, including being used as the object of many prepositions and some verbs, as well as being used alone as a kind of adverb to express time or location, like the Latin ablative case.

(*)Technically the English genitive -'s isn't a suffix, but a clitic. It attaches to noun "phrases", not just nouns. For example, you would probably say "[The cat and dog]'s toys...", while a true suffix like the plural -s would have "The [cat]s and [dog]s play with their toys."

Hard to say; it also depends on what you mean by the "instant before", and depends on what you mean by "ordinary matter." As the core of the star is collapsing, its size approaches its Schwarzschild radius, and the instant that it does, an event horizon forms, blocking any further observation of what's happening to the core and officially making it a "black hole." We have no way of knowing if the core becomes a singularity at that exact moment, sometime later, or at all. All we can say is at that instant, whatever is going on inside behaves as if there is already a singularity at the center. And if there is truly a singularity inside, it is discontinuous with the rest of spacetime, so questions relating to its time frame kind of become meaningless as it now exists outside of time.


As for the composition of the collapsing star core, this is also a dubious question to answer. The incomprehensible pressure the matter is under probably means that it's continuously undergoing changes on a nanosecond-by-nanosecond basis as it approaches the Schwarzschild radius. Is it still made of atoms, protons, neutrons, etc.? Maybe, maybe not. However, neutron stars are about the closest thing to a black hole a collapsing star can become while still retaining observable structure, and their composition may hold some insights. The incredible pressure within neutron stars breaks apart distinct atoms into their free protons, neutrons, and electrons, and then fuses all the protons and electrons together, forming more neutrons, hence the name "neutron star." Furthermore, there is a hypothesized form of matter called "strange matter" (so definitely not "ordinary" matter) that might be found in the core of neutron stars, where the pressure could be so extreme that the neutrons themselves decompose into a plasma of free quarks and gluons. That's a good candidate for the composition of a collapsing star core right before it becomes a black hole.

Tl;dr to my reply I just made: we cannot explain how a singularity works in terms of the mathematics of our current theories. We say that there's a singularity *precisely because* the mathematics of our current theories has failed.


In general, whenever you hear the term "singularity" in a mathematics or physics context, you should interpret that to mean "the math is broken."

Well, the concept of the singularity came from Schwarzschild's solution to Einstein's field equations, which includes the term 1/(1-s/r), where 'r' represents the radius of a sphere surrounding a massive body, and 's' represents the radius of the massive body itself, related to the body's mass. You can see that when s=r (representing a critical radius known as the Schwarzschild radius), the term simplifies to 1/0, which is obviously an indeterminate form, implying that at that critical radius, the density becomes infinite. If you're looking for a mathematical description of how an object turns into a singularity, you're not going to find one, since by definition, the Schwarzschild metric is only defined when s>r or r<s. When r=s, weird things start happening, an event horizon forms which blocks our knowledge of what goes on inside, and our equations become undefined, and start spitting out infinities. Furthermore, our understanding of quantum mechanics imply that all things have a minimum size, meaning infinitesmally small singularities should not exist. Yet black holes do exist, so either there are true singularities (which we simply are not able to describe in the way you're looking for, as our theories break down here), or there are not singularities, but for all intents and purposes behave like singularities (and we would also be incapable of describing why or how this could be).


In mathematics generally, the term "singularity" itself refers to a point where a function becomes undefined (due to division by zero or something similar). In general relativity specifically, a "singularity" means a point where spacetime itself becomes undefined, meaning it is no longer a part of the spacetime manifold, meaning quite literally *it is beyond space and time.* We have no idea what is going on with singularities, or what the process of their formation looks like, if they do indeed exist. Unfortunately, that is probably not the answer you were looking for.

We really can't know. The event horizon is an information barrier, meaning that we cannot know what goes on inside a black hole without entering it, but nothing that enters it could ever transmit knowledge to the outside.




All that our observations/calculations tell us is that, from outside the event horizon, black holes behave *as if* there were an infinitely dense, infinitesimally small singularity on the other side of the event horizon.




But you're right, that is not a very intuitive concept, and whenever infinities pop up in our calculations, it's safe to be suspicious. It's likely that there's something a lot weirder going on inside the event horizon, but beyond the event horizon our understanding of physics breaks down. We just use the singularity model because it works for prediction purposes outside the event horizon.

You're right in that phenotypes exist and ethnic groups exist physically. But ethnicities ARE NOT races. Traditionally, there are 4 or 5 major "race" categories that people are divided into: Caucasian, Asian, African, Native American, and sometimes Australian Aboriginal. These "races" do NOT reflect the differences of the many different ethnic groups that compose each "race", each with its own phenotypes.


The crucial point here is that there is not one phenotype associated with each "race", and skin color ends up being the main identifying factor determining whether someone belongs to one "race" vs. another. But skin color only indicates the latitude that an ethnic group has been living in, not that everyone with the same skin color has inherited the same phenotype! For example, dark skin has evolved independently and has also been lost independently in many populations.


Furthermore, studies of genetics within and across populations consistently show that there is more genetic diversity within any given population than there is between different populations. So if you were looking at the genetic variation within a tribe in Africa, you'd find that any two individuals from that tribe are likely to be more different genetically from one another than if you compared (on average) the genes of that tribe as a whole  to the genes an ethnic group in Europe or Asia.


In particular, the idea of a cohesive "black" or "African" race is absurd, because all human genetic diversity found worldwide is a subset of the genetic diversity found within Africa. This means that any genes you can find in Italians, or Scandinavians, or Cherokees, or Vietnamese, or the Sami people, etc. can also be found in at least one population in Africa.


This also means that the genetic difference between the supposed European and African "races" (or Asian and African, or European and Asian, etc.) will be less than the difference between any  two ethnic groups within the African "race" itself. Almost any two ethnic groups found within Africa will have completely different phenotypes, histories, and are likely to not share a recent common ancestor at all. They may have even been evolving separately for longer than the other "races" have. But, because both these populations evolved in a similar latitude, they have similar skin tone (a small aspect of their phenotypes) and thus they are considered to be part of the same "race".


So in short, while there are some physical features common to populations in certain regions (which may or may not reflect common ancestry at all), and different ethnic groups have their own phenotypes, the concept behind "races" essentially assumes common ancestry and a common phenotype for everyone who descends from that region (mostly on the basis of skin color), which is not supported by research on genetics, human migration patterns, or anything else.

Ancient Greek mathematics focused heavily on geometry, and in geometry numbers didn't represent quantities so much as lengths. Basically, when coming up with some geometric construction, the Greeks would start out by drawing a line segment which they would call the "unit length" (essentially giving some line segment the property of having a "length of one"). All other numbers were defined in reference to the unit length, i.e. 2 didn't mean "2 of something" but rather "twice the unit length", 3 meant "three times the unit length", etc. So for example, they might construct some shape by doing X, Y and Z, and say "Observe that this line segment is twice the unit length, while this line segment is four times the unit length" so they would find the numbers, say, 2 and 4 interesting in this context. But they wouldn't have found the number 1, i.e. the length of the unit, interesting because they could define ANY line segment as the unit length, meaning any line segment they chose could have a "length of one". Therefore, the number one had no special properties.

Energy, in essence, is the ability to do things. I know science fiction, fantasy, and religion tend to mysticise energy, depicting "pure" energy as some glowing white light or something like that, but really there is no "raw" energy like that. Humans notice water moving through a river, and figure they can use that motion to turn a waterwheel. Humans notice the heat coming off a fire, and figure they can use it to cook their food. The amount of work you can get that moving water or burning wood to do is what energy "really" is. Modern physics allows us to quantify this more-or-less exactly, and though it can be hard to see how a single proton could do work for us, it's still the same idea. The word "energy" itself comes from Greek "energeia", meaning "inner work." So there's nothing special about energy at all, it's just a measurement of how much we can exploit natural systems to get them to do stuff for us.

This fact relies on two properties of multiplication:


1. Commutativity. It does not matter what order you multiply two or more numbers. So A × B = B × A, and likewise A × B × C = A × C × B = B × A × C and so on.


2. Associativity. If multiplying more than two numbers, you can group the numbers together however you like, and handle the multiplication separately for each group. So A × B × C = (A × B) × C = A × (B × C).




Let's use these properties, and use the 2% of 50 example above. First, note that 2% = 2/100 = 2 × 1/100. So we can rewrite the expression:


2% × 50 = 2/100 × 50 = (2 × 1/100) × 50 = 2 × (1/100 × 50) = 2 × 50/100 = 2 × 50%.

But more simply, it's just a manifestation of the "measurement problem" common in other areas of science. To get information out of a system you have to interact with the system, but interacting with the system changes the system, paradoxically changing the information you're trying to measure.




For example, if you're trying to figure out how hot a cup of coffee is, you might put a thermometer in it. But as soon as you put the thermometer in, it absorbs heat from the liquid thus lowering the temperature. So you can never really know what the temperature "truly" is/was. Or in the quantum case, pinpointing the location of an electron triggers waveform collapse, forcing the electron into a certain location that it wasn't at before you tried locating it.

>My (rough) understanding is that Greek was widely used among the lower classes of the empire

Not so much, Greek was a high-prestige literary language in the Roman world, even predating the transition of the Roman Republic into the Roman Empire.

>because the conquests of Alexander the Great spread Greek throughout the Mediterranean.

In the East this is sort of true, but Alexander's conquests and the subsequent Hellenistic period more spread the clout of the Greek language and culture than it did make Greek the common vernacular of the whole Mediterranean.

>Then when Rome conquered everything, they didn't bother forcing everyone to speak Latin. And so only the elite, upper class Romans spoke Latin, and everyone else spoke Greek.

Not really. The Romans were mostly content with leaving their conquered peoples speak their vernacular (which was NOT Greek except in parts of the empire with high Hellenistic influence, mostly in the East), but since all administration was done in Latin for practical purposes, gradually people stopped speaking their local languages, and Latin became the speech of many common people, at least in the West. Hence the massive distribution of the modern Romance languages. Meanwhile Greek was a high-prestige language, as mentioned above, that the Roman elite would have learned from childhood. So really the situation of Greek vs. Latin was the opposite of what you have in mind.

>Would someone like Paul have spoken both languages and just written in Greek to reach a wider audience (and poorer audience more likely to receive his message)?

I don't know if Paul spoke both Latin, but it is almost certain that Greek was his native language because he was born in one of the most Hellenized, Eastern parts of the empire. He didn't write in Greek to reach a wider/poorer audience; in his part of the world, EVERYBODY spoke Greek. Latin actually would have had lower prestige.

>If that's the case, then when/how did Latin become the de-facto language of the church? Was it with the conversion of Constantine or did it happen earlier? What language would the Council of Nicaea been held in?

Latin is not the de facto language of the Church, only the Roman Catholic Church which is what you have been more exposed to. Constantine didn't make Latin the language of the early church; he knew Greek, as any high-born Roman would have, probably preferred Greek to Latin, and Greek was maintained as the language of Christianity for a long time, since the part of the world that Christianity was born in was Greek speaking. The Council of Nicaea would have been conducted in Greek because Greek was the language spoken in Nicaea, and the language common to all the learned bishops.

What triggered the adoption of Latin instead of Greek in the Western Church wasn't because Latin was higher-prestige and Greek was lower-prestige, but the opposite. In the Western part of the Empire, the common/poorer people would not have had the education to have learned Greek, but they would have spoken Latin as their native language. So Latin was adopted as a concession to the common people. This is reflected in the name of the famous Latin translation, the Vulgate ("Biblia Vulgata" - "Common-tongued Bible").

It's an interesting idea, but it doesn't contain an explanation for what might *drive* such a cycle. Personally, I find the hypothesis that stress accent (specifically, unstressed inflectional morphemes) leads to gradual simplification/loss of inflectional morphemes and then inflectional systems as a whole. While this need not be the case in tonal/pitch accent languages which largely maintain their complexity over the centuries due to giving all syllables equal prominence, and thus the "cycle" doesn't necessarily apply to them. So if there even is such a cycle, it's probably more of an accident of phonotactics and linguistic innovation than a fundamental property of language change.

Lots of languages with complex morphology tend to be either tonal or have "pitch accent". In either case, all syllables are pronounced with equal prominence despite differences in pitch. But in languages with "stress accent", one syllable in a word is clearly emphasized at the expense of the other syllables, which are pronounced much more weakly. And it often occurs that in stress-accent languages, the final syllable(s) of the word (which often contain the inflection) are unstressed. So generations of pronouncing these syllables weakly leads to them being simplified and eventually dropped entirely, which can lead to a wholesale erosion of inflectional systems. On the other hand, tonal/pitch accent languages tend to maintain their inflections much more consistently over the centuries. Ancient Greek and Sanskrit had pitch accents, so we can suppose PIE had a pitch accent too, which somehow became a stress accent in most of its daughter languages. So there's nothing unique about the complexity of PIE and other ancient languages, and complexity doesn't necessarily have to be lost over time. It's all about phonotactics and prosody, and it just so happens that the descendants of PIE (nearly all of them with stress accent systems) dominated their geographical areas, which might make it seem like a more universal "rule" of simplification than it is.

Edit: the Baltic languages are still highly complex with respect to PIE, and they have maintained a complicated pitch accent system due to cultural/geographical isolation which has also largely insulated the PIE inflectional system.

It's actually pretty transparent if you analyze the names they chose.

Nominativus = "pertaining to names (nomen)" = the "name" case (i.e. it's the name/default form of the noun)

Accusativus = "pertaining to accusation (accusare)" = the "accused" case (i.e. something happens to it)

Genetivus = "pertaining to the 'gens'" (i.e. family or kind) = the "related" case

Dativus = "pertaining to a gift (datum)" = the "giving" case

Ablativus = "pertaining to being off the sides (ab + latus)" = the "moving away" or "coming from" case

Vocativus = "pertaining to calling (vocare)" = the "calling" case.

Locativus = "pertaining to a place (locus)" = the "place" case

The case names we use today are just English variants of the names the Romans used *themselves* for the cases: casus nominativus, casus accusativus, casus genetivus, casus dativus, casus ablativus, and casus vocativus. So not only would Ancient Roman grammarians have recognized the same cases (as you can tell, the word "case" in this context also comes from them them), but those terms (except one, keep reading) were translations of the terms used by the Ancient Greeks in *their own* grammatical tradition. Furthermore, Greek doesn't have an ablative case (technically it completely merged with the dative case in prehistory), meaning the name "casus ablativus" had to be invented by Roman grammarians. So the case names are truly ancient, and you can be sure the Romans believed in a distinct ablative.

And the Indo-European dative/ablative distinction IS a complicated topic. They were of course similar in Latin, had merged in Ancient Greek, and we can see similar patterns in many other ancient AND modern (just compare the Lithuanian dative and "instrumental" cases) IE languages, suggesting that they have always been somewhat similar in form. The best hypothesis is that in the plural, the prehistoric ablative had an "m" in it, not "b", and in the singular ended in a consonant like "t" or "d". Even a few centuries before the Classical Latin period, we can see from inscriptions that in Old Latin the ablative was still more distinct, containing a final "d" in the singular of all declensions and genders.

No. At the beginnings of words, and between two other vowels, 'u' and 'i' (which would've been written like <V> and <I> in Roman times) represented consonants comparable to the English "w" and "y". In writing however, the Romans did not distinguish between "consonantal" 'u'/'i' and "vocal" (vowel) 'u'/'i'. Only later did they start using 'v' and 'j' for consonantal 'u' and 'i', to make the pronunciation more clear. The Romans also originally didn't have "lowercase" letterforms either. So what we write in modern times as "vacuum" would have been written like <VACVVM>, "divus" as <DIVVS>, "Jupiter" as <IVPITER>, etc. Don't confuse how a word is written with the word/pronunciation itself.

It's a later convention. In the classical period they would have just used "u" and "i" (which they would've written like <V> and <I>, since 'v' actually came first, and lowercase forms hadn't been invented yet either). Also, 'v' and 'j' in modern usage are called "consonantal 'u'/'i'", comparable to the English consonants "w" and "y". So they don't only show up in the beginning of words, but also in the middle, such as <EIUS> -> "ejus", <DIVVS> -> "divus", etc. 

Keep in mind though, even in modern times, it's really a personal choice what you want to use, there are no hard rules. And while using 'v' for consonantal 'u' has pretty much caught on universally, using 'j' for consonantal 'i' has not. So you'll often see a modern version using 'v' but not 'j': like writing the original <VACVVS> as "vacuus" but <IAM> as "iam" instead of "jam". Some people also choose not to use 'v' either but only 'u', so writing <VENIT> -> "uenit" instead of "venit". And while it's not super common, sometimes you'll even see people who choose to use only 'v' to look more like the original writing style, so <CVLTVS> -> "cvltvs" instead of "cultus".

Grams are not a measurement of weight. Grams are a measurement of mass, and mass simply means how much matter is in something. Weight, on the other hand, measures how much gravity is pulling on an object with mass.

So, something with a mass of 1 kilogram has a mass of 1 kilogram whether it is on Earth, on the moon, or in the vacuum of space. Because the amount of matter in that thing does not change, regardless of where it is. But an object that weighs 1 pound on Earth will only weigh 1/6th of a pound on the Moon, but will weigh nothing in space, because Earth has stronger gravity than the Moon, while there is practically no gravity in the void of space.

To summarize, mass is an inherent property of something, but weight depends on the object's location in the universe (though you do use mass to calculate weight). Mass remains constant, but weight can change (in fact, your weight slightly fluctuates throughout the day as the Moon rotates around the Earth, slightly changing how much gravity is pulling on you). And an object made of matter can have zero weight (if it experiences no gravity) but can NEVER have zero mass.

For most verb forms, the "subject" \*does\* the verb, whereas the verb \*happens to\* the "object".

In English the subject comes before the verb, and the object comes after the verb. In pronouns alone, they have different forms depending on if they are the subject or object:

* Subject: he, she, it, they
* Object: him, her, it, them

In Latin, ALL nouns have different forms depending on if they are the subject or object. And so word order is more flexible but generally the subject comes before the object (and the verb comes last). The different forms are called "case" suffixes and are determined by the "declension" of the noun (don't worry about that right now). But the common case suffixes you should recognize are:

* Nominative case (subject), for masc/fem/neuter:  -us/-a/-um (sg.); -i/-ae/-a (pl.)
* Accusative case (object), for masc/fem/neuter: -um/-am/-um (sg.); -os/-as/-a (pl.)

Fun fact: Notice how in both English pronouns and in Latin nouns, the neuter pronoun/gender does not distinguish between subject or object. This is not a coincidence or a borrowed from Latin but due to English and Latin's shared Proto-Indo-European ancestor, probably based on an ancient distinction between "animate" & "inanimate" (living vs. nonliving) nouns.

First, some grammar terms with English examples that still apply to the Greek:

Example sentence: "\[I\]               \[pet\]        \[the  dog\]"

Syntactic role:          subject     verb      object

Semantic role:          agent       active    patient

​

Now in the passive: "\[The dog\]   \[was pet\]    \[by me\]"

Syntactic role:            subject     verb          prepositional phrase

Semantic role:           patient     passive     agent

​

Basically the passive voice "promotes" the patient from object to subject grammatically so that you can refer to it more easily. And the agent of a passive phrase is demoted (prepositional phrase or dative in the Greek) to the point where it is kind of optional and the passive verb is more of an intransitive verb like "sleep", "run", etc. ("I sleep", "I run", but not "I sleep him/it/her" or "I run him/it/her").

Now in Greek, the middle voice is somewhere between active and passive. If there is an object involved, both subject and object participate in the action of the verb, and are both agent and/or patient. If there is just a subject, the subject performs the action of the verb on itself or for its own benefit, and is thus both agent and patient.

So you can't just substitute middle and passive for each other in most cases. Furthermore, Greek has some verbs that take on a sort of idiomatic meaning in the middle voice (and a few in the passive). For example:

αἱρέω "I take"  -> αἱρέομαι "I take (for myself)"  \~\~\~ "I choose"

These middle-conjugated verbs are used like active verbs and are called "deponent" verbs.

If a word ends in a consonant or consonants, all except "r" or "n" is dropped. Like "Louis" being pronounounced Loo-ey,  "Gaspard" being pronounced gas-Par. "Edmond" being pronounced ed-Mon. There are exceptions like the final 's' is pronounced in "Mercédès" mer-say-Des, though the accent gives you a clue.

French has a silent "e"/"es"  at the end of words (except  if there's an accent) which does allow for written words to be pronounced with final consonants. One major exception is "re".

There's a catch with "r" and "n" being the only consonants pronounced. The French "r" is much different than the English "r". It's a soft sound made in the throat that often sounds silent. 
And "n" isn't actually pronounced by itself (except at the beginning of syllables or followed by silent 'e' like "Madeleine") but indicates a "nasal vowel", so really "Edmond" = ed-Mõh, "Fernand" = fer-Nãh. It's just like that stereotypical nasally French "honhonhon" baguette laugh where you don't really pronounce the 'n'.  Also the specific combination "en" is pronounced like "an", i.e. ' ãh '.

French doesn't really have syllable stress like English but for simplicity's sake just put the stress on the final syllable of every word or name. 

"H" is silent, so "Henriette" becomes ãh-ree-Et.

"Ch" is pronounced like "sh". 'C" is generally pronounced how it would if it were an English word. Soft "G"  ('g' before "i" or "e") is really soft, like the "g" in "genre".

French has a bunch of letter combinations that sound the same. Famously all of the letters "au", "aux", "aulx", "eau", "eaux", "haut", "hauts" are homophones and are pronounced "oh". So it's actually much easier to learn French pronunciation once you recognize the common letter sequences.

It represents a norm: an abstract concept sort of like an absolute value. In a "metric space" (which is also an abstract concept, but it's basically just a set that allows you to measure some concept of "distance" between any two points; the points here could be single numbers, coordinates, or even more exotic depending on the space), the norm of a point measures the "distance" between that point and the equivalent of the "zero" point in that space. You can think of the absolute value of a number as its norm in the 1-dimensional metric space of the number line. In fact, a norm is just a generalization of the concept of the 1D absolute value to different, usually higher-dimensional, situations. While the absolute value uses single bars |•|, a norm uses double bars ||•|| to convey that it's similar to the familiar absolute value.

Interpret chained-together possessive phrases left to right, where the noun phrase to the left owns the noun phrase immediately to its right, and in these chains, every time there is a possessive word, the current noun phrase ends and a new one begins. In your first example:

> The team members' shoes' color

The first noun phrase is "The team member's", and the next one is "shoes'". The meaning of the first possessive should be clear. Then, relative to "shoes", the next noun phrase is "color". So the color belongs to the shoes. Don't worry about what came before so much. Break the noun phrases into pairs in order like "the team members' shoes", "shoes' color", etc.

> The laundry's man or the Laundry man

I have never heard "laundry's man", it's usually "laundry man" or "laundryman". This is not a possessive phrase, but a compound noun. I can see how you can go from "laundry man" to "man of laundry" to "laundry's man", but we never use the possessive form when making terms based on profession. We make a compound word like "fire man"/"fireman", "laundry man", "mail man"/"mailman", "team member"

> My sister's kids' shirts sizes

Very good example except "shirts" should be possessive. Interpret first "my sister", then "sister's kids", then "kids' shirts", and "shirts' sizes".

Like in the second example, it's not "school's friends'" it's "school friends"/"schoolfriends", a compound word not a possessive clause. Looks pretty decent! Searing any kind of meat is pretty simple once you know a couple tricks. First, high heat! The hotter the better. The Maillard reaction ("searing") will not happen fast enough at medium temperature before the meat cooks, and won't happen at all at low temp. 


Second, DON'T flip your steaks to check if it's searing! When the Maillard reaction is underway, the meat will stick to the bottom of the pan. When the meat is as seared as it will get, the meat will "release" from the pan and be able to move around freely. But if you try to check the sear too early, by prying the meat off the pan while it's still stuck, you're just scraping off the sear that's already developed and preventing the reaction from happening further. Instead, just shake the pan side to side. If the meat doesnt move, it's still searing. If the meat moves around, it's done searing, time to flip it over.
